title: Do This If You Want Another Year of Windows 10 Security Updates
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Michal Krakowiak/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

title: The iPhone X Literally Changed How We Use Our Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: AFP contributor / AFP via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET, and Popular Science.By 2017, some of us had been using iPhones for 10 years—a whole decade building muscle memory, all of it based around the Home button. Press once to go home; press twice to open the app switcher; long-press to call up Siri; press in tandem with the power button to take a screenshot: These actions became so innate, you didn't think twice about using them—at least, not until the Home button disappeared. 
That was the year Apple released the iPhone X, introducing the device's most radical change since its first iteration. (Perhaps only to be surpassed this year by the iPhone Duo.) It's funny to think about it today, but back in 2017, the iPhone X's single pane of glass was disruptive, to say the least. Where was the Home button? Without it, how could you do anything? That confusion inspired Lifehacker to publish "The iPhone X Gestures You Should Master," a guide to navigating your newly designed iPhone. 
We had to learn to swipe up from the bottom of the display to go home; to swipe along the bottom to switch from app to app; to swipe down from the top right to access Control Center; to swipe down from the top left to access Notification Center. We even had to relearn reachability: Instead of lightly double-tapping the Home button to bring the screen down, you had to swipe down on the bottom of the display. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Reviewing these things now, it all seems so obvious, even second nature. Nearly another decade has passed since we published that story, and by now, most iOS users are accostumed to a Home button-free life. But looking through the comments on this nearly decade-old piece, it's clear the transition was anything but smooth. One user complained about how smartphone gestures were making everything more confusing. Another bemoaned how switching between their iPhone and iPad meant jumping between two different gesture systems. Fast forward to 2026, and it's near impossible to imagine going back. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple didn't immediately stop making iPhones with Home buttons—it also released the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus the same year as the iPhone X—but the writing was on the wall. Soon after, only the SE line shipped with the old design, and even iPads adopted an edge-to-edge display. With the launch of the iPhone 16e in 2025, Apple officially retired the once-essential Home button. Though you can still buy and use second-hand devices that have one (the 2022 iPhone SE can even run iOS 27), it's clear the company has moved on, and the gestures once so foreign they once prompted us to publish a guide to their use are now as innate as doing things the old way. Perhaps in another 10 years, wearables and hand gestures will have changed everything again, and we'll look back with nostalgia on an era when we had to touch our devices at all.

title: Apple Is Bringing Back an Apple Watch Feature It Took Away With watchOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 22, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            With watchOS 27, Apple inexplicably removed the app switcher from Apple Watches.
                                            The feature is back with watchOS 27.2, which is currently in beta testing.
                                            Since this is the beta, there are no guarantees the feature could make it to the official build of watchOS 27.2.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Typically, software updates introduce new features rather than taking them away. So, when you install watchOS 27 on your compatible Apple Watch, you probably aren't surprised to see updates like Siri AI or a step counter on the watch face. But you might be taken aback by what's missing—a multitasking feature that your Apple Watch has had for years. watchOS 27 removed the app switcher on Apple Watch As reported by 9to5Mac, Apple quietly removed the app switcher from Apple Watches with watchOS 27. As a result, users running the beta over the summer, or those who updated in September, were likely confused when double-clicking the Digital Crown: On watchOS 26 and earlier, that gesture pulls up a menu with all open apps, similar to the app switcher on iPhone. This allows you to quickly return to a previously used app without needing to dive into the "honeycomb" main app menu.With watchOS 27, that's no longer the case. Not only is the app switcher gone, but the honeycomb app menu has been sidelined. In their place, Apple is pushing its new "Dynamic app grid." When you press the Digital Crown once, you'll see this new menu, which features the apps Siri thinks you're most likely to use. That might include recently used apps, but also apps you frequently use, even if you haven't used them in a while. 
That might prove to be useful. The honeycomb menu can certainly make apps difficult to find, especially if you have a lot of them on your watch. But replacing the app switcher entirely doesn't make much sense: There's no guarantee Siri is going to list the recently used app you want to use on the new menu, so you might be forced to manually hunt for it anyway, whereas with the app switcher, you could quickly bounce back to any app, provided you had opened it recently. This isn't the only feature Apple removed with watchOS 27—the company also discontinued the Walkie-Talkie feature with the update. But it looks like it won't be gone for long.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The watchOS app switcher is coming backIt seems Apple is changing its mind (or coming to its senses): 9to5Mac recently spotted that the app switcher is back as of the watchOS 27.2 beta. Apple didn't make a note of the addition in any changelogs, so it's unclear why the company undid the change, but it's a welcome recursion—though at this point, there's no guarantee it will make it to the official build of watchOS 27.2. If you're hoping for similar news about Walkie-Talkie, unfortunately that feature has officially been discontinued, so don't expect to see it in a future update.
    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

Speaking of which, the only way to try watchOS 27.2 now is to install the watchOS beta on your Apple Watch. That's a risky venture, since you can't downgrade back to watchOS 27 if something goes wrong. Still, if you're really missing the app switcher, you can get it back by enrolling your watch in Apple's beta.

title: 10 'Homebrew' Hacks Every Mac Power User Should Know
description: Homebrew is the package manager you wish your Mac shipped with. Once you set it up, Homebrew lets you install and update apps quickl
body:
Homebrew is the package manager you wish your Mac shipped with. Once you set it up, Homebrew lets you install and update apps quickly and securely. It launched as a command-line interface, where you would type commands into the Terminal app on your Mac to install, update, or uninstall your apps. Recently, Homebrew launched its own GUI, which makes it easier than ever to use the service. Here are 10 Homebrew hacks that you should know, great for new and legacy users alike.Try Homebrew's new GUI to discover apps
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you update to Homebrew version 7.0.0 or newer, you'll notice that the service has a new GUI-enabled app for your Mac. You can launch it like any other app from the Applications folder, and use the interface to discover, install, update, and remove apps. The left pane has a few tabs that allow you to keep tabs on apps you've installed via Homebrew, updates available for those apps, fixes for issues with installation, and Homebrew settings. It also has an option called "Discover," which lets you search for apps available to install via Homebrew. Just use the search bar to look for your favorite apps, and if they show up, click the "Install" button. This will download that app to your Mac, and automatically complete the installation.Check out Homebrew's "doctor" to fix software issuesHomebrew has a "doctor" feature that lets you fix issues with the service. This can be anything from unsupported or deprecated apps, to issues with the Homebrew configuration itself. You can run this from the "Doctor" tab in the Homebrew GUI, or use the following command via Terminal:
brew drThe service will recommend some fixes, and you can run the suggested command in Terminal to solve the problem.Use the -q suffix to keep Terminal free of clutterWhen you're using Homebrew via Terminal, you'll quickly notice that every action leaves you with a wall of text. This is great for those who want to track all those updates, or those who are roleplaying as characters from The Matrix, but not for everyone. If you want Homebrew to do its work quietly, just add the "-q" suffix to your commands. For example:brew install firefox -qThis will minimize the number of text updates on-screen, and leave you with a much cleaner Terminal. If you'd like to see more updates, you can replace "-q" with "-v" at the end of the command.Try the "list" command to view all installed apps via Terminal
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
If you're not using Homebrew's GUI, it's easy to forget which apps you installed via Homebrew, and which ones are outside of it. To solve this, use the following command to show a list of all apps installed via Homebrew:brew listUse this command to add manually installed apps to HomebrewIf you're like me, you've probably installed some apps via Homebrew, and downloaded a few others from the developers' websites. This means you can't update all your apps in one go, since some of them are not managed by Homebrew. You can fix this issue by adopting those apps into Homebrew. Use the following command to get this done:brew install cask adopt APPNAMEAs long as the apps are supported in Homebrew, this command will adopt them into the service. You can confirm the adoption by using the "brew list" command mentioned above.Use the cleanup command to free up storage spaceWhen you install a lot of apps via Homebrew, it tends to create some clutter. Old versions of apps and cached downloads aren't always deleted immediately. If you're running short on space, you can try the following cleanup command to free up space without deleting apps:brew cleanupUse this Homebrew command to update all apps in one goThis is one of the best features in Homebrew, and it works best right after a new version of macOS is released. This is when a flurry of app updates arrives to support the new operating system, and you can try this command to update all Homebrew apps in one go:brew upgradeIn case you just want to see which apps need an update, you can try this command:brew outdatedThe upgrade command is also listed under the "Upgrades" tab in the Homebrew GUI.Use "dry run" to check which packages will be installed or updatedIf you add the "dry run" flag to any install or update command, it will reveal a list of planned updates without commencing the installation. When you're dealing with command-line interfaces, "dry run" can be a useful way to preview changes before they take place, and to ensure that the correct app is being installed or updated. This is how you can use it:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
brew install APPNAME --dry-runSet up aliases to avoid typing long commandsIf you're tired of typing long commands in Homebrew, you can set up aliases to minimize keystrokes. For instance, you can use "brew i" instead of "brew install" to update all Homebrew apps. Use this command to set this up:brew alias i='install'Feel free to set up aliases for as many Homebrew commands as you like. The following command will list all the aliases you've set up:brew aliasTo remove an alias, use this command:brew unalias iJust remember to replace "i" with whichever alias you wish to remove.Use this command to stop specific apps from updatingIf you don't want to update to the newest versions of certain apps, you can use the "pin" command to stop updates, and then "unpin" when you are ready to update again. This can be useful when an app you trust gets acquired by new owners who have yet to prove themselves, or if it adds new features you don't want, etc. Here's how to use it:brew pin APPNAMEWhen you're ready to update it again, try this:brew unpin APPNAMENote that you may also have to disable auto-updates from the app's interface separately because some apps just update themselves without confirmation.

        Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H. Right now, this 2026 model is down to $1,049.99 on Woot, which is its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. The same system is listed on Amazon for $1,697.99 (down from $1,997.99), so not only is the discount substantial, but Prime members also get free shipping (everyone else pays a $6 delivery fee).
Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

        There's a reason Bissell's Little Green Machine has a dedicated following among pet owners (not to mention kid owners): It's a powerful upholstery cleaning tool that can do the work of an upright steam cleaner, and can be carried in one hand. But there's an even more compact version, the Bissell Little Green Mini Portable Carpet Cleaner, that's just as powerful and even more portable, making it an especially good bet for, say, cleaning out your car after taking your dog on a long road trip. Right now, you can grab one for $89.99, 10% off the usual price, straight from Bissell.As the name implies, this thing is small. It weighs in at only seven pounds, making it the lightest and most compact carpet cleaner in Bissell's lineup. It's easy to take it up or down stairs, into a car, or anywhere else around the house you need deep-cleaning power. You fill up the water tank, add cleaning solution, spray the stain, scrub it with the attached tool, and the machine will suck the dirty liquid back into a separate tank.The Little Green Mini is great for pet messes (I've used it on the rug more times than I'd like to admit), spills, stains, and dirt on carpets, rugs, and furniture. Because of its small size, it's also easy to stow away. It includes a four-inch Tough Stain Tool, a hand-held attachment to scrub the affected areas. The water tank can hold up to 16 ounces, and the dirty water tank, 13.5 ounces—pretty small, but that's the tradeoff for more portability. The main hose is four feet long, and the power cord is 12 feet long. It comes with an eight-ounce bottle of Bissell Little Green Oxy formula for cleaning, but when that runs out, you can use most any carpet cleaning solution you want..If you don't need or want a massive machine to clean your messes, or want something portable to go up or down stairs or that fits easily into a vehicle, the Bissell Little Green Mini Portable Carpet Cleaner is a great option at the current 10% discount.

            Credit: StackSocial
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Buying a six-year-old refurbished MacBook in 2026 obviously isn't the right choice for some, but for this sale price of $279.99 at StackSocial, it can make sense for a student, casual home user, or anyone who needs an inexpensive secondary Mac for browsing, documents, email, streaming, and video calls. This is the Intel version rather than the better-known M1 model from later in 2020, so expectations should remain reasonable. It uses a 10th-generation Intel Core i3 processor with 8GB of RAM and Intel Iris Plus graphics, which is fine for writing in Google Docs, keeping a handful of browser tabs open, joining video calls, or watching Netflix, but it's not something I would buy for video editing, modern games, or heavier creative work.Still, the hardware has the sharp 13.3-inch Retina display, the Magic Keyboard is comfortable to type on, and Touch ID makes logging in and approving purchases easier. You also get two Thunderbolt 3 ports, USB-C charging, and a 720p webcam. Apple originally rated this model for up to 11 hours of wireless web use, although a refurbished battery that is six years old may not come close to that figure. StackSocial lists this particular machine as Grade B, so light to moderate scuffs are possible, and the included warranty lasts 30 days.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The bigger concern is how long it will stay useful. This MacBook Air can run macOS Sequoia, but it doesn't support macOS Tahoe 26, so it's already missing out on Apple’s latest major operating system update. That doesn't make it unusable, but it does limit how much life you should expect from it going forward. At $279.99, I would consider it a short-term option for a student, someone who needs a secondary laptop, or a casual user who mostly browses the web, streams video, and works with documents. It makes much less sense for anyone who wants a MacBook to keep for several more years, especially when newer Apple silicon models offer better performance and longer software support.

title: I Just Bought a House, and I Want to Make It the Coolest One in the Neighborhood
body:
Jordan Calhoun
                            
        
            Jordan Calhoun
                
                                            Editor in Chief
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJordan Calhoun is Editor in Chief at Lifehacker and author of Piccolo Is Black: A Memoir of Race, Religion, and Pop Culture. He holds a BA in Sociology and Criminal Justice, a BS in Psychology, and an MPA in Public Policy.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 11, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Jordan Calhoun / Lifehacker
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        After years of city living and renting, I finally bought a house. And, as any homeowner will tell you, buying a house means taking on a large, time-consuming, expensive responsibility. I plan to share that adventure over on our social media pages, but with a twist: You can expect home maintenance content, but I also want to make this the kind of house I wanted as a kid. You know, like when you visited your friend who lived in the coolest house in the neighborhood.

I have a long list of small projects I've been putting off, like fixing my running toilet or cleaning my garbage bins so bears and flies stop coming around; but I also have fun projects that I want to try out, like installing permanent outdoor lights, designing a reading nook, converting my garage into a home gym, and turning my basement into a home theater. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As I enter my influencer "like and subscribe" era, I invite you to follow along on our official Instagram, official YouTube, or my personal page. And if you want to browse any of the products I use to do the projects yourself, you can find an ongoing shopping list, organized by project, on one convenient page. I'm looking forward to the hard work...I think. I'll see you here and on our social pages.
